decisions.reason: SOL drops the distance unit *li* from the image.
SOL keeps the proverb and no-exaggeration sense in natural prose.
SOL preserves the scene and breaks the long sentence cleanly.
SOL keeps the eagles’ departure and flight toward separate destinations.
SOL preserves the red-stained snowfield shrinking to a drop of blood.
SOL keeps the repeated passage of day and night and the plateau’s disappearance.
SOL drops the established term “messenger eagle” and the source’s dozens.
“Come out” preserves the urgent call to leave the house.
SOL keeps the differing arrival times and the crowd’s response.
SOL preserves the before-dawn disturbance and the sleepers’ bewilderment.
The source says “someone else’s house,” not “my house.”
SOL changes the timing: people grabbed collars before anyone thought to answer, not before asking questions.
SOL keeps the excited crowd shouting repeatedly as it drives away the dawn.
“What nonsense” fits the speaker’s response and preserves the interruption.
SOL drops the speaker’s tentative “yet, have you?”
“Wiped out to the last man” preserves the source’s total-annihilation emphasis.
“Highborn or lowborn” naturally preserves that shock was the same regardless of status.
SOL keeps the remote peasant’s poverty and knowledge of Dark Heaven.
SOL preserves the Demonic Cult’s infamy and the comparison with Dark Heaven.
“Sought the world itself” drops the source’s explicit aim to obtain or claim it.
SOL keeps the two-character explanation and the threat to dynasty and peace.
SOL removes the explicit identification of Dark Heaven and the crowd’s ongoing cheering.
SOL keeps the question about the victory’s scale and the crowd’s excitement.
SOL preserves the question waking the speaker and the proud reply.
SOL drops the speaker’s audible gasp at the number.
SOL’s “far beyond the ranks” is an awkward recast of the huge headcount exceeding that of a mere cult.
SOL keeps the half-day and hundred-thousand claim; “know” is sufficient for the acquaintance.
“Crushed” preserves the claim that more than a million rebels were annihilated.
SOL keeps the objection that a million is too many while preserving the incredulous tone.
SOL preserves the self-correction from half a million to three hundred thousand.
SOL keeps the challenge about where the number came from.
SOL preserves the interrupted objection in natural dialogue.
“Is that up to me?” keeps the speaker’s helpless question.
The source begins with “Ah,” not the more forceful declaration SOL gives.
SOL preserves the stammer, reluctant agreement, and request to calm down.
SOL keeps the crowd leader’s instruction and the slogan.
“Speak up” naturally conveys the complaint that the response is too quiet.
“When does this end?” keeps the exasperated question.
SOL preserves the correction from the epithet to the marquis’s title and the warning to prepare.
SOL keeps the reluctant minority and the common folk’s unrestrained cheering.
SOL preserves the striking change in public opinion over only a few years.
“Power had harbored injustice” is an awkward collocation; “bred injustice” keeps the source’s causal sense.
SOL preserves the rhetorical question and its image.
SOL keeps the stagnant-water image and the absence of perfect good or evil.
SOL keeps the turn to the present.
SOL preserves the wonder at how much one person changed.
SOL awkwardly makes the footsteps themselves fall “deep and vast”; BASE keeps the path’s giant-like scale.
SOL preserves the family’s rise across Shanxi and the northern grasslands and its place among the Five Great Families.
SOL keeps his lineage, role in the Alliance, martial prowess, and fight against Dark Heaven.
The name is clear from the preceding context; SOL avoids needless repetition without changing the claim.
SOL preserves the lack of doubt or resentment about the epithet’s weight.
“No one dared” keeps the emphatic refusal to challenge him.
SOL removes BASE’s redundant “eyes” while keeping the proof witnessed by many.
SOL naturally connects the point to his standing beyond Murim.
SOL drops the proclamation’s imperative “hear this.”
SOL deletes the source’s standalone “Son of Heaven” title.
SOL incorporates the Son of Heaven into the following sentence and preserves his mandate.
SOL preserves the Emperor’s revelations, appointment, declaration, and dismantling of the barrier.
SOL keeps Jin Taekyung as the Emperor’s battering ram.
SOL says the rebels wield supernatural powers, where the source says they dare defy the order and seek to wield them.
“Shaking” replaces the source’s image of the name resounding across the regions.
SOL preserves his two public roles and the Great General’s work putting down traitors.
SOL keeps the contrast between martial artist and Emperor-appointed marquis.
SOL preserves the unprecedented appointment and his fight to end the chaotic age.
SOL keeps the repeated victory.
The source praises the Emperor’s reign without explicitly calling it wise; SOL avoids that addition.
SOL softens the explicit insistence on getting drunk to merely having a drink.
SOL preserves the story’s embellishment and the undeniable victory.
SOL keeps the packed taverns, revelers spilling outside, and toast to Gansu’s victory.
SOL preserves the praise, thanks, and relief without BASE’s awkward “as one.”
SOL keeps the tentative hope that the war will end soon with little harm.
SOL drops the source’s urging to hurry.
SOL adds “all of it,” intensifying the instruction beyond the source.
SOL preserves the laughter, feasts, and absence of fear.
SOL carries the martial artists and common folk into the next sentence without losing the contrast.
SOL keeps both groups laughing and celebrating their victory.
SOL preserves the one-day qualification and the ominous pause.
SOL keeps the falcon’s origin in Qinghai’s distant western frontier and its weary arrival.
SOL drops that the forgotten dream was from the previous night.
“Exciting story” keeps the imagined appeal of the dream.
SOL folds the learning transition into the next sentence.
SOL keeps the link between forgetting a dream and avoiding a nightmare’s lingering feeling.
SOL preserves that forgetting did not mean the nightmare never happened.
SOL keeps the waking, swaying saddle, Hyuk Mujin, and the offered cloth.
“What’s this?” matches the question about the cloth; SOL instead asks its purpose.
SOL keeps the dry retort and refusal to wipe him down.
SOL preserves the vivid feeling of wet clothes clinging to him and the cold sweat.
SOL adds “what it was,” spelling out the terse “I know” thought.
SOL naturally identifies the two categories as kinds of people appearing in his nightmares.
SOL keeps the people’s deaths caused by his failure to save them.
SOL preserves the contrast with people killed by his own hand.
SOL’s “again” implies recurrence; the source says another kind was added after a long time.
SOL moves the strange, unexplained dreams into this line instead of preserving the sudden recollection.
SOL deletes the distinct image of a strange, unidentified dream.
SOL preserves both identities and the memories of the Taiyuan Jin Taekyung’s past.
SOL keeps the thought that the current dream might resemble those memories.
SOL preserves the overhead birdcall interrupting his thought.
SOL keeps the contrast between the present and the dream’s illusory quality.
“Now’s not the time” keeps the brief self-reminder.
SOL preserves the small head shake and the drawing up of Scorching Yang Qi.
SOL replaces the source’s “tuduk” sound with “drip.”
SOL invents drops falling away; the source only gives a sound effect as the clothes dry.
“There’s that way too” preserves Mujin’s realization.
SOL drops the teasing “unlike you” jab.
“Showing off” naturally conveys the question about bragging.
SOL keeps Mujin’s resigned concession.
SOL shortens the established name Hyuk Mujin to “Mujin.”
SOL drops the skyward look and the source’s unthinking reaction.
SOL keeps the prompt widening of his eyes.
SOL preserves the blood-soaked missive tied to the falcon’s leg as it glides overhead.
